sections.heading: Coming back to your mercy at the end of the day
sections.text: My Father, if your mercy had a limit, I would have nowhere safe to go. Your judgment is not unfair, and my sin is not small. But your love for me in Christ is deeper than my failure, and it does not run out. So tonight I come to you again, not hiding, not pretending, but looking for shelter in the mercy you have shown through your Son.
theological_themes: God’s mercy is the sinner’s only refuge from deserved judgment.
The believer approaches God as Father because of God’s immeasurable love in Christ.

scripture_references.connection: Paul grounds salvation in God being rich in mercy and acting toward sinners through Christ. This supports the prayer’s confidence that God’s love in Christ is larger than personal failure.
The verse declares that those who are in Christ are not under condemnation. That directly undergirds coming to God for refuge instead of fleeing from him in fear.

sections.heading: Naming my sin honestly before you
sections.text: I bring myself to you with the sins I committed today and the good I failed to do. I have sinned against you, my Father; against you, my Redeemer; and against you, Holy Spirit, when you were warning, pressing, and leading me. I have gone against what I knew in my conscience, against the clear teaching of your Word, against my neighbors, and even against my own soul. Please do not deal with me according to what I deserve. I have no righteousness of my own to offer you, and I have no excuse that can cover what I have done.
theological_themes: Sin is against God first, while also harming others and the self.
True confession includes both sins committed and duties neglected.
The sinner cannot stand before God on the basis of personal righteousness.

scripture_references.connection: David recognizes that his sin, though it deeply harmed people, was ultimately against God. This supports the prayer’s Godward confession without denying the damage done to neighbors.
James names failure to do known good as sin. That gives biblical weight to confessing both wrong actions and neglected obedience.
The psalmist asks God not to enter into judgment because no living person is righteous before him. This closely matches the prayer’s refusal to plead personal merit.

sections.heading: Resting in what Jesus has already finished
sections.text: Forgive this day, which has been stained by evil. Tonight I renew my repentance before you. I keep beginning the day with real desires to love you more deeply, serve you more honestly, live more fully for you, and belong to you without reservation. And still I stumble so quickly. I drift. I find again how weak, needy, and sinful I am. But I thank you that the finished work of Jesus does not need my achievements added to it. His offering is enough. His sacrifice has answered for my sins in a way my best efforts never could.
theological_themes: Repentance is renewed, not as self-salvation, but as a return to God.
Christ’s finished sacrifice is sufficient for sin and needs no human addition.
The believer’s assurance rests in Christ’s work, not spiritual performance.

scripture_references.connection: Hebrews contrasts repeated sacrifices with Christ’s once-for-all offering, which fully accomplishes what is needed for those who are being sanctified. This grounds the prayer’s confidence that Jesus’ work needs no supplement.
John holds together honest confession of ongoing sin and God’s faithful forgiveness. This fits the prayer’s evening repentance without despair.

sections.heading: Asking for real change, not just regret
sections.text: If you give me more days, help me to change. Teach me to hate evil, not excuse it. Help me run from the very sins I have just confessed instead of circling back to them. Make me firmer in obedience, more awake to danger, and quicker to pray. Do not let evil grow from the seeds I have planted today. Stop the consequences of my careless words, choices, or attitudes from spreading farther than they already have.
theological_themes: Genuine repentance seeks practical amendment of life.
Growth in holiness requires watchfulness, prayer, and God’s help.
Sin can bear fruit beyond the moment, so the believer asks God to restrain its effects.

scripture_references.connection: This proverb connects mercy not only with confessing sin but also with forsaking it. That supports the prayer’s request for change rather than mere remorse.
Jesus tells his disciples to watch and pray because human willingness is real but weak. This speaks directly to the prayer’s request to become more watchful and prayerful in the face of temptation.
Paul teaches that what a person sows bears a corresponding harvest. This illuminates the prayer’s concern that sinful choices may produce damaging consequences unless God mercifully restrains them.

sections.heading: Wanting my life to help others, not trip them up
sections.text: If today I was ashamed of Christ or of your Word, forgive me. If I was unkind, bitter, envious, cold, careless with my speech, or quick-tempered, do not let my sin become a reason for someone else to harden their heart or think less of your name. Please make my life straighter and cleaner than it has been. Let my example quietly challenge what is wrong, make goodness attractive, and show that the ways of Christ are truly beautiful.
theological_themes: A believer’s conduct can either adorn or dishonor the gospel before others.
Love of neighbor includes concern not to become a stumbling block.
Christian holiness should display the goodness and beauty of Christ’s ways.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that visible good works should lead others to glorify the Father. This supports the prayer’s desire for an upright example that honors God.
Paul warns believers not to put a stumbling block in another person’s way. This grounds the prayer’s concern that personal sin not harden or mislead a neighbor.
Paul says faithful conduct can adorn the doctrine of God our Savior. That supports the prayer’s request that the believer’s life make the ways of Christ look as lovely as they are.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original speaks of God’s 'just wrath' and the believer having no righteousness of their own. I preserved this rather than softening it, while framing the prayer within refuge in Christ so it remains pastorally and theologically balanced.
The original addresses sin against the Father, the Redeemer, and the Holy Spirit. I retained this Trinitarian shape without over-explaining it or turning the prayer into a doctrinal formula.

The concern that one person’s sin may harden a neighbor reflects a strong view of moral influence and public Christian witness. I rendered it as a request that God restrain the damaging effects of the speaker’s conduct.
significant_interpretive_choices: 'Sins of commission and omission' was rendered as 'the sins I committed today and the good I failed to do' to keep the concrete moral scope of the original in natural speech.

'His oblation is sufficient satisfaction for my sins' was rendered in terms of Jesus’ offering and sacrifice being enough, preserving substitutionary atonement language without using archaic sacrificial vocabulary.
'Let no evil fruit spring from evil seeds my hands have sown' was kept as a concrete sowing-and-fruit image, because the original’s concern is not only guilt but the ongoing consequences of sin.
'Lovely are the ways of Christ' was interpreted as the moral beauty and attractiveness of life under Christ, not as a promise that obedience will be socially admired.
